topic: The iPhone Upgrade Spiral vs Android Drift
description: From 2016–2025, track how iPhone monetization and share shifted during the upgrade slump, while Android brands fractured and later re-accelerated—ending with 2025’s mixed performance as the smartphone market rebalances.
youtube_description:
📉📱 This chart-race turns the smartphone story into a money race.

You’ll watch 4 forces compete from 2016 → 2025: Apple’s upgrade-by-services flywheel, Google’s ad engine (which increasingly shapes Android demand), Samsung’s profit volatility, and Huawei’s collapse after export restrictions.

04:30 2022–2023: Huawei falls off a cliff
05:40 2024: Apple’s services keep rising

• AppleSvc accelerates as iPhone upgrades slow but Services deepen.
• GoogleAds grows even when hardware growth is uneven—capturing attention monetization.
• Samsung swings with the premium/discount cycle.
• Huawei drops sharply post-2019–2020, never recovering to its prior scale.

instagram_caption:
🚀 The $300B smartphone momentum question: who really “won” 2016–2025?

For years, the iPhone story was simple: sell the hardware, then make money on upgrades. But the real twist? The upgrade spiral didn’t just stall—it transformed. While iPhone unit growth got choppier, Apple built a second engine: Services. In our timeline, Apple’s Services run-rate jumps from about $22B (2016) to ~$46B (2019), then surges from $56B (2020) → $68B (2021) → ~$79B (2022) → ~$86B (2023) → ~$96B (2024) → about $108B by 2025. That’s a classic “hardware slows, profit migrates” play.

Meanwhile, Android didn’t collapse—it fragmented. Google’s ad revenue shows why: even when device upgrades don’t move, attention monetization can. Google Ads rises from ~$79B (2016) to ~$116B (2018), then explodes from ~$147B (2019–2020) to ~$210B (2021) and up to ~$275B by 2025. The Android ecosystem got monetized through apps, search, and ads—so the “winner” isn’t always the handset brand.

Samsung tells the rollercoaster version. Its smartphone profit proxy hovers near $16B–$20B (2016–2019), peaks around $25B (2020), then dips to ~$21B (2021) and falls sharply to ~$12B–$16B (2023–2024), before a modest recovery to ~$18B in 2025. Premium cycles came with harsher competition and faster churn.

And then there’s Huawei—the dramatic exit. Starting around $65B (2016), it slides to ~$55B (2017) and ~$41B (2018), then crashes to about ~$12B (2019), and nearly evaporates by 2020 (~$0.8B) and remains ~200M by 2024–2025.

So here’s the question for you: In this iPhone upgrade spiral, was the biggest winner Apple… or the Android ecosystem’s monetizer (Google)? Drop your pick: Apple, Google, Samsung, or Huawei.

facebook_caption:
From 2016–2025, smartphone “competition” increasingly became a competition over monetization, not just devices. Apple’s iPhone upgrade spiral gradually shifted profit toward Services: Apple’s Services run-rate grows from ~$22B in 2016 to ~$108B by 2025. This matters because even when handset demand becomes uneven, recurring services revenue can keep compounding.

On the Android side, Google’s advertising revenue shows why the ecosystem remained powerful. Google Ads rises from ~$79B (2016) to ~$275B (2025), indicating that engagement and ad monetization can keep growing even as hardware cycles fluctuate.

Samsung’s handset profitability behaves like a cycle: roughly ~$16B–$20B (2016–2019), a rise to ~$25B (2020), then a downturn to about ~$12B (2023) before partial recovery by 2025 (~$18B).

Huawei illustrates the extreme outcome. Its smartphone revenue proxy falls from ~$65B (2016) to ~$41B (2018), then drops to ~$12B (2019), and collapses to ~<$1B by 2020—remaining near ~$0.2B by 2024–2025.

Which phase do you think mattered most for the smartphone market: Apple’s Services pivot, Google’s ad dominance, Samsung’s cycle volatility, or Huawei’s exit?
threads_caption:
The “iPhone upgrade spiral” wasn’t really about upgrades—it was about where the money went. 👀

Apple’s Services basically kept climbing (from ~$22B in 2016 to ~$108B in 2025), even as the hardware race got messier.
Google’s ad engine also kept growing (to ~$275B by 2025), so Android didn’t need to win every phone battle to win monetization.

Samsung? More of a rollercoaster. Huawei? Straight-up fall off a cliff.

Which would you rather have been in 2019–2021: Apple, Google, Samsung, or Huawei?
